utterances.text: [Interpretation] The order was given. Milan Lukic was telling this man named Razonoda, Lelek , that the police were no good, were not effective in a way, that they weren't getting anything done and that he had to do the whole job himself. He was shouting, yelling at him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And who was Razonoda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a local policeman from before the war. I can't remember his real name, but that's what everybody called him in Visegrad. He was very tall, over two metres probably. He worked as a policeman before the war, and he worked at the station where they held me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was there any other occasion on which you heard Milan giving orders to anybody at the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Whenever he needed a set of keys or something, he would never ask nicely. He would order them to bring a set of keys so he that could get into a cell or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And were these orders given to policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: VG-89, I'd like you to take a look around the courtroom here today. Aside from myself and Mr. Groome and Mr. Zec, I was wondering, is there anyone that you recognize in the courtroom here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes. I recognize the second man on the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have to wait for the transcript to be restarted. There's a technical problem. We can resume now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: VG-89, could you please look around the courtroom and let the Chamber know if you recognise anyone here today besides myself, Mr. Groome, and Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes. The second person from left to right, to the left, wearing what I think is a pink shirt and a black jacket. That's Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What row is this person sitting in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Third row.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect the identification of the accused Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Standing objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is the accused that you identified here in court today, Milan Lukic, the same individual that you saw on the 21st of May, 1992; early June 1992 during your bus convoy; the 12th of June, 1992; and the 14th through the 17th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I would object to the leading nature of the questioning and also misrepresentation of the evidence as the 21st of May. He was 150 metres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We note the objection. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: VG-89, my name is Jason Alarid, and I represent Milan Lukic [Realtime transcript read in error, "Mr. Lukic"]. Can I ask you a few questions about your testimony today and your statements that you've already given in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, I would like to start talking with -- about your time at the police station, the MUP building. Just by what you were able to observe through the cell doors, of course on your arrival and other things, how many different police officers do you think you saw over the course of your three days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Perhaps about five, six, or seven different ones, those that I was in touch with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you say police officers, how would you separate someone as a police officer from being a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Policemen had that blue police uniform while the rest were wearing camouflage. There were many local police officers there, such as Lelek, Tomic, Dragan and others. I knew them because they worked for the MUP, and I lived two streets away from there, used to live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, but could my learned friend Mr. Alarid precise which client he represent because on page 47, line 8, is not clarified, so just the full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You heard that I represent Milan Lukic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you say that you lived a couple blocks from the MUP building, you had seen certain police officers for quite some time, including Tomic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: That's right. Tomic interrogated me at the MUP building. That was before the war and also before I ended up there. Yes, I used to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and that's what I recall from one of your statements is that soon after you were brought from the bridge to the police station you spoke briefly with Dragan Tomic, the commander.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: 17.45 in the afternoon, the 14th of June, on the first floor in Dragan Tomic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when -- isn't it true that you knew that you were going to be interrogated by Dragan Tomic before 17.45?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What time did you know that you were going to be interrogated by the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: When one of the policemen came, opened the door, and led me away, he told me we were going upstairs to the office of Dragan Tomic, chief of police. I was being taken there to be interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Mr. Lakic who released you, what uniform was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Camouflage army uniform. That's what he was wearing when he came to the prison that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what about Chief Tomic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: He was in civilian clothes, a suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So if I understand you, during this time police officers wore the regular blue uniform but sometimes also changed into camouflage, and then with regards to the chief he was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's a compound question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will allow it. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who changed into what, but I know about the policemen I had known from before the war, that I used to see them wearing blue uniforms. During my stay in gaol, they were wearing blue police uniforms, and Dragan Tomic was the only one in and suit. I didn't know the others who visited. All I know is they wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I guess I'd like to focus on Mr. Lakic, only because you saw him in a camouflage, but you also knew him as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I did not know him as a police officer. As far as I remember, he was not a police officer before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But with him being at the MUP building during that time, could you assume that he was a police officer during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: In that MUP building I saw him only once, in the morning of the 17th. He was wearing a camouflage uniform. He hadn't been there. Otherwise, I saw him just that once, and I know for sure he wasn't a policeman before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, before your testimony today did you review both your 1995 statement as well as your 2001 statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When you looked at your 1995 statement, did you notice that you had used the name Dragan Lakic as the person that had released you as opposed to Mirko Lakic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Maybe I made a slip of the tongue or maybe the person who took the statement made a mistake. Dragan Lakic is Mirko Lakic's son, but he's not the one who released me. I was released by Mirko Lakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Understood. I just didn't know what it was. Now, when you were in the cell right before you were released, it appeared that Milan Lukic did defer or take orders from Mr. Perisic. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was your understanding -- well, in your statement of 2001, you indicated that you knew who Perisic was and Dragan Tomic in advance as being associates. How did you know them to be associates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I knew Dragan Tomic because I lived close to the MUP, and I used to see Perisic around town, but I didn't know him personally. All I knew is that he was a teacher. I was just finishing my eighth year of primary school, and I was supposed to go on to secondary school where he taught. What kind of friends they were, I don't know. I used to see them together at the MUP. When you see people together, I don't know what it looks like to you, but it looked to me that they were friends or they had some business together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you know, and I do understand that you were a young boy at this time and you may not have known a lot of the political situation as the war started, but did you have any understanding even from talking to your older relatives or friends that Mr. Perisic was the commander, even a superior to Dragan Tomic during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you find it funny, though, the money that was being collected in the cell from you and your cell-mates was being ordered to be given to Mr. Perisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I thought it was too little money for Lukic, for Milan Lukic. That's why he wanted Perisic to have it. If there had been more money, I'm sure he would have taken it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But is it a possibility that in fact Mr. Perisic was the one entitled to it regardless by virtue of his being a superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I heard - not saw - I heard that Perisic took money from Muslims who had the money, who could afford it, in exchange for taking them out of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what was your understanding of this payment that was made by your countrymen to escape Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Well, they usually asked wealthier people to pay so that their lives be spared. I don't think Milan was engaged in that. I think he was engaged in other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I guess my next question to you would be, then, if Mr. Perisic is the one that has the authority to -- the authority to give these passes to the wealthier Muslims, wouldn't that indicate that he's in a position of authority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Perisic was not the only one who could do that. Any Serb at the MUP could take the money and get someone out of the town. It wasn't only Risto Perisic. He was not the only person who was being obeyed. Milan and Lakic and anybody else could do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, just backing up to the very end --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When you escaped to Bosnian territory and you left the bus, there's a mention in your 1995 statement that Stanko Pecikoza was in camouflage and driving one of the buses and also fired at Muslims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Pecikoza was the name, but he didn't drive a bus. He drove a truck. He started shooting when the Muslims tried to save some people because they knew that people -- Serbs from the -- Serbs were going to take out some people from the first convoy as they had done before and kill them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you were taken to the office of -- of Dragan Tomic, would it be fair to say that he was in charge of the -- of the MUP? He was clearly the commander-in-chief of the police there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's how it looked to me, and that was true, I think, because he was the only one in civilian clothes, and he was the one who interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say, although you saw such horrible things during your stay there, it was Dragan Tomic that was the only one that actually hurt you or hit you during your stay at the MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you indicated on your -- in your second statement that -- that you came to the police station on the 14th because -- you remember this because of a soccer game that you were going to watch on TV that night in the European Championship. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I remember it by many things. The European Championship is just one of the many things why I remember that. It's not only the European Championship. That date was memorable to me even before Milan Lukic took me to the bridge. It was memorable because my mother stopped working that day. Among other things, she did not dare go to work any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the day -- that day was a Monday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly if it was Monday, but I know that my mother was supposed to go to work but didn't because Serbs had already started killing everyone indiscriminately. She didn't dare to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is it -- is it true that your -- or you tell me. Would your mother normally work on a Sunday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: She worked almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But in your statement of -- of 2001, you indicated that the -- one of the reasons that you remembered it was the 14th is because Germany was going to play that evening. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you with any certainty that Germany was playing that evening. In any case, we were rooting for Germany because when I was giving those statements, I did not speak any English. Some people interpreted, and I didn't understand what they were saying, but I was rooting for Germany. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, the only reason I say this, I can only read what was in English, and it appears that you were going to watch the Germany game on television that evening, and that's the reason I'm asking you these questions. But if I were to tell you that I looked on the schedule for the European Championship, Germany was to play on the 15th, Monday night, would that change your perception of what day the 14th or the 15th is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: No. No, it wouldn't. I remember very well that it was the 14th, and we rooted for Germany that European Championship; at least, I did. Whether they were playing that day or another day, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could the court usher -- assistant please bring up what has been uploaded as 1D10-1679, being the English version, and 1D10-1690, which is the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the Prosecution could just be informed; what version of what document are we referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It's the 2001 January statement by the witness to the ICTY, and I would focus the attention on page 2 of the English statement as well as the B/C/S statement, bottom paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, sir, is that your signature at the bottom of the English, understanding you don't read and write English, but is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I'd like you to read the bottom paragraph of this statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: "Samir Dervisevic got killed later in June along with another friend of mine from Foca whose last name I don't know who was living temporarily with the Koric family in Visegrad. I witnessed two killings at the new Drina Bridge on Saturday, 14 June 1992 [as interpreted], around 1600 hours. I remember this date because it was during the European football championship in 1992, and that evening there was a match with Germany that we wanted to see on television." Somebody misinterpreted this. It was during the European Championship, and we did root for Germany, and we watched the European Championship even after leaving Visegrad for Visoko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, during this answer there was a reference to Saturday, the 14th of June, 1992. I don't know if that was a mistake in translation and reading from the document. I do notice that the document may say something different. If we could please just clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, may I just ask the interpreter what does the B/C/S say?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The B/C/S says Saturday, 14 June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Sir, was it Saturday, Sunday, or Monday? Sir, I'm sorry, did -- maybe you didn't hear me. Was it Saturday, Sunday, or Monday, because there was something in the translation. Maybe you misread your statement, but I will tell you your statement says Sunday the 14th, remembering it because of the championship, but I'm simply going to ask you: Was it Saturday, Sunday, or Monday when you were -- when this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, there was -- there was also someone else there, going backwards from your release, that allowed you some food and water. His name was Lalo. How did you know Lalo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: It's another misinterpretation. The name was Lelek. His name -- his full name was Zeljko Lelek.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was he another police officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: As far as I know, he started working as a policeman just before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony today you mentioned that this person that you knew as Milan Lukic shook your hand on two occasions, the second one wearing a gold ring. Do you realise that at no time before did you mention two times in which Milan Lukic shook your hand, and you never mentioned a golden ring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: That golden ring I noticed that second time when he shook my hand. He may have had it before without me noticing, but the second time I noticed it, all right. Huge ring, yellow gold.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you agree in having reviewed your statements that you only mentioned a single time in which Milan Lukic shook your hand and then told you that you were not to be harmed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: At the time when I was giving my first statement in 1995, in my country the war was still raging, and the people who wanted me to make that statement, I had never known them before, nor did anyone from my family, so I gave that statement to people I didn't know during the war under huge pressure and -- of fear. I had no idea what could happen to me if I gave that statement to people I didn't know, and I didn't know who they were working for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did they appear to be helpful, like they were police authorities that wanted to find the perpetrators of the -- the crimes in, around Visegrad that you might have witnessed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes. It appeared to me that way, but I wasn't really sure where I was going because the war was still going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you were safe in Muslim territory, and you were being interviewed by Muslim police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: You are never safe from the Serb army and Serb paramilitaries. They kept shelling Sarajevo, and it was up the shelling that I went to that interview. I risked my life, actually, to reach that place where the interview was to be conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And might I ask you how -- how did you come into the radar? How did -- how were you brought to their attention as a witness to the crimes in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection. That calls for speculation as to what those individuals thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the second aspect of the question, yes, but how did you come into the radar? Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those people that I didn't know found me in Sarajevo. I have no idea how. Until that moment, I had not told anyone anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would it be better to say that you had not told any authorities about it, but I'm sure you had discussed it with family and close friends of your family what you had gone through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: When a man kills two children in front of you, of course you keep discussing it throughout your life with your family and your friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, during your stay in that gaol cell, were there other cells around you, or was that the only detention cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I didn't walk around, and I didn't go to other cells. I was in that one cell throughout the time. I went sometimes to the reception desk, and I went to Tomic's office upstairs. I don't know about the rest of the layout.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is the reception desk on the ground floor, what I would call the first floor, but I know many people call the second floor the first floor. Was it on the ground floor, the reception area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: So when you go through the entrance door of the MUP building, you walk up the steps, about ten steps, and on your right-hand side from the staircase there is a reception desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in your statement, the gentlemen that you indicated held a knife to your throat and threatened you, took you out of the cell and threatened you. In your statement, you indicated it was four to five police officers, but today you indicate that it was gentlemen wearing JNA uniforms, and I'm just asking if you understood the men in JNA officers to be police officers, or if they're different.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: These men who took me were wearing olive-green/grey uniforms, characteristic for the JNA, and they had knives and bayonets, and one of them with the Serbian accent put a bayonet to my throat, and his accent was from Serbia proper, not from one of our localities. That's what I said even the first time when I gave a statement. I don't know how it was translated to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, what I have in English is that this was a younger one, 20 years old, that held the knife to your throat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Correct. I had never before seen policemen wearing green camouflage uniforms and carrying bayonets, and that man was a young man, 20ish, wearing a green -- olive-green/grey uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, did the incident where you were threatened to cut your throat, was that before or after --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, was the incident where you were threatened to cut your throat before or after the Milan Lukic associate came in and told you how Muslims were killing Serbians in nearby villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so now you say that -- but if I were to tell you that in your statement you indicated that the man that came in and spoke to you about Muslims committing violence was actually at 2.00 in the morning on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: That's what I said to you. That man came late at night. It was very dark. Whether it was 2.00 a.m. or 1.00 a.m. or midnight, I didn't have a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in your statement, though, it indicates that the next morning is when those four or five police officers who you now say were in JNA threatened you and -- to cut your throat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: That same morning before this Milan Lukic came in the evening with his Chetnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: In your statement, you don't mention that Milan Lukic accompanied this associate on that single occasion. Is it your testimony today that he was with him and you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. If counsel just could please reference which statement he's referring to. There's two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The 2001 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I ask you again, that isn't it true that in your statement you did not mention that Milan Lukic accompanied this associate on that single occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I heard Milan Lukic's voice. I didn't see him. He didn't come to the detention unit that night. He didn't mistreat anyone, but I could hear him in the hallway. The younger man who came along with him was the one who entered the cell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not the point. What counsel is saying, that in your statement, the 2001 statement, you didn't mention that Milan Lukic accompanied this associate on that single occasion. The point he's making, that you didn't mention it in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Lukic was there that evening. He just didn't actually go into the cell in which we were. He was out in the hall where the cell was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And before either of these occasions, isn't it true that there was one moment where four -- five or six soldiers disguised with stockings and masks covering their faces came into the cell and began beating the other inmates, not you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Every night they came and beat the other prisoners - the 14th, the 15th, and the 16th - but not me. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What were these masked men wearing as -- as uniforms or clothing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I really didn't have a chance to look closely, but as far as I could tell they were wearing camouflage, and for the most part they were hitting people with their rifle butts. Again, I wasn't really in a position to do anything else but just keep my head down and stare at the wall. There were some situations in which Lelek took me outside the cell while they were beating all the other people in there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is that more than one time that you were allowed to be removed from the cell during these beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I was once allowed to leave; they were spending the night, and then another time when they gave them some food and allowed them to use the facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you indicated that your mother was aware that you were under arrest and actually came to question why and visit you during this time period. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I saw my mother for about two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And if I might ask you, was your father in Visegrad at this time, or was he somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: He was elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you indicated that your mother was outside the cell window, but it's my understanding that the cell window is very high off the ground, maybe three metres, and would be very difficult to look out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: No, not quite. Not three metres. It was lower than that, and it's not like I really used that window to look outside very much, nor was I allowed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when these policemen or soldiers would come in to beat people, did you see anyone giving orders within those groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: No, I didn't, nor was I in a position to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How many people total --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How many people were detained with you in that cell over those three days, different people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Eight at the very most. At one point there were eight. They would always take someone out or bring someone new. Eight was the maximum for as long as I was there. When I left, there were only two persons remaining inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did this Razonoda ever participate in these beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It's my understanding that many Muslim cars and property were seized during this time. Do you have knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: By all means. Everything we had was taken from us, our lives included.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you see a group of Muslim vehicles at the police station when you were brought there, other Muslim vehicles as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: No. I saw nothing. I was in no position to see anything. I'd been brought back from facing a firing squad. It wasn't like I'd just been back from a football game or a trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Early on in your stay there, you saw other police officers beat a man severely and then use a walkie-talkie to talk to other police officers as they looked for the man's son. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you please describe what these -- this group of police officers was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: They weren't all wearing the same clothes, this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, one of the things on the bridge that was unclear to me is that when you arrived on the new bridge this Milan Lukic said, if you -- stay in the car, to the other two soldiers, if you have -- if you don't have the stomach, but you didn't describe how three boys got out of the vehicle with those two soldiers staying in the car. Did they get out and get back in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: We got out of the car, the three of us, Samir on the right, and I and the lad from Foca got out of the left-hand side of the car, the driver's side. As for the question, Milan told those rather young Serb soldiers as follows: "If your heart is faint, stay in the car." It wasn't us that he told to stay in the car if we so wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's not what I meant. I meant that the soldiers in the back did get out of the vehicle. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Do you think you could have 70 persons leave the back seat of the vehicle without anyone moving? There were seven of us there. Of course someone had to move over for someone else to leave. What I'm telling you is that they didn't leave the car. They stayed in the car when Milan took us away and this guy that he was with. We couldn't just leave the car by miracle without having them move over for us to be able to get out, could we?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, going back to when you came to the understanding of who Milan Lukic was. Isn't it true that you had heard stories about Milan Lukic before you had ever had an understanding of who he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: The first time I heard of him was when we were supposed to go to Macedonia, when my friend's sister addressed him by name. That's when I heard his name for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so as you gave statements after the fact, you mentioned that a Milan Lukic was both -- was at the funeral of Behija Zukic, but the trip to Macedonia happened after of that date. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the person, but I didn't realise at the time that he was Milan Lukic, just like I saw him when we were supposed to leave for Macedonia, but I wasn't actually aware of this until my friend's sister called him by name. I saw the man, but I didn't know his name. It wasn't until later that I learned his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so at the Behija Zukic funeral, you were a hundred and fifty metres away from the TAM truck and the Lada that came. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, yes. I can't be more specific about the distance, but that's the ballpark.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you have binoculars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so isn't it true that the only reason that you believe that a Milan Lukic was at the funeral is because you understood the TAM truck to also have been owned by Behija Zukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that. I did know that the Passat belonged to Behija Zukic, and I only found out later about the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How did you come to believe or to know that Milan Lukic was at the funeral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw a man leave the driver's seat. This was the man, 195 centimetres tall, wearing camouflage, black hair, and right next to him that same person who had taken us to the bridge, one rather short and the other rather tall. And then when we were supposed to go to Macedonia, when we were off I realised that this was the same person because I finally had a chance to see him close up, and that was when I concluded that this is the same person that I had seen before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could the court assistant please bring up what's been uploaded as 1D10-1664, being the 1995 statement and the -- and, Your Honour, this is -- the problem with this is this is one we did not get the Bosnian translation for, and we had requested it, and that was I think one of the things that might have been pending before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It was my understanding that we tendered both versions on the 4th of July, 2008. However, we're going to check right now just to confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If not, I do have a B/C/S version available for counsel here today to use in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So let him have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, Mr. VG-89, what I've handed you is what I believe is the B/C/S version of your 1995 statement. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, the paragraph that I handed or at least instructed the court assistant to look at starts with the date the 20th of May, 1992, Behija Zukic, the owner of a private shop. It's actually the next paragraph related to the next day, the 21st of May, 1992, that I'd ask you to look at, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It should be the very next separate paragraph saying, "While the funeral of Behija, Medo, and his wife at the town cemetery ..." and it goes on from there. And a little later, it states that, "Milan Lukic along with a group of his Chetniks arrived at the cemetery gate in a white Lada and a green two-and-a-half ton TAM truck, which he had stolen from Behija."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And for the court assistant, that is on page 4 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And considering that this happened before you knew who Milan Lukic was from your sister's friend, that's why I'm wondering if you're just assuming this later because of what you heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: No. Later, after all of this when we had reached free territory, I found out about the TAM truck. That's when I gave my statement, and that's when I found out that the TAM had belonged to the Zukic family. While all this was going on, I didn't know, but I included this in my '95 statement because in the meantime I had learned who the truck had belonged to, but that wasn't before '95.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So isn't it true that at a hundred and fifty metres different, it would be very difficult to identify a single person that you did not know before and never had seen before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Well, maybe it wasn't all of 150 metres, but I had a clear view of who was leaving that truck and how those people were moving, especially because having left the truck, they stood there for quite some time waiting for those people to return. It wasn't like they were standing outside the truck for a mere one or two seconds. They actually spent some time standing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, we have to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. VG-89, what I'd also like to point out is that in your 1995 statement, you also included a Mitar as being someone you were able to see from a hundred and fifty metres away. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would the court assistant please bring 2D01-0143 and 2D01-0152, which are the simultaneously B/C/S and English versions of the 1995 statement, and I'd like to direct him to page 5 of the English statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you can look, sir, do you still have the paper statement in front of you of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could you turn to roughly page 5 to the first mention of the 12th of June, 1992. Actually, the question I was going to ask you was with regards to the incident with -- with Kasim, and in your statement -- in your statement of 1995, you indicate that the person that you knew as Milan Lukic had a short machine-gun, not a sniper rifle, as you testified today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection. That misstates what the statement says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what does the statement say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could direct counsel's attention to the third line in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Armed with a light machine-gun. Light machine-gun. I'm sorry. I said short.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your testimony today was that during that incident the person that you knew to be Milan Lukic had a sniper rifle, yet in your statement of three years after the incident you indicate he had a light machine-gun. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: No, it wasn't a machine-gun that he had. He had this rifle, a sniper rifle. I don't even know what a machine-gun looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But isn't it true that you did read and sign that statement in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the best time to correct those kinds of situations is when you're signing something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: That's right. But I didn't read it or correct it. There were some mistakes concerning the translation from Bosnian into English, concerning some names and, as I now realise, some developments, but I haven't looked at this statement for years. I don't think I ever actually read the entire statement. If I had at an earlier stage, I probably would have made a number of suggestions to them about possible corrections such as this machine-gun detail. I don't even know what a machine-gun looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But I would point your -- a little further down in the paragraph, you indicated that in fact you had an understanding or knowledge that Kasim was killed by Dragan and Boban Tomic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: This is something I heard after I'd left Visegrad, but I saw Milan Lukic take him away. I didn't see for myself who killed him. I just heard from the other Muslims that Dragan and Boban Tomic had killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did they give you any details beyond that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Not that I remember. I wasn't there myself, so I can't really say. Perhaps they did mention something else but nothing that I remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could the court assistant please back up the English version to page 4 and direct the B/C/S version to the paragraph where it says, "The next day, May -- 21st of May 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, isn't true that in this paragraph you indicate that you recognised Mitar, a waiter in the Visegrad hotel, despite being a hundred and fifty metres away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I didn't say that I recognised him at the time, not at the time. I didn't recognise Milan Lukic at the time, either. I realised that this was the same person when I was off to Macedonia. I didn't know at the time who he was, and the same applies to Mitar. My friend and I were saying that this was a waiter from Panos. Mitar is someone I never saw from close up. Therefore, I wasn't able to guarantee 100 per cent, but we just heard that this was a waiter from the Panos cafe. It wasn't until later on that I saw Mitar around town when he forced me to sweep the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And can you tell me when Mitar forced you to clean the streets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: It was before we left for Macedonia. Mitar was carrying an armband with a Red Cross or something, the civil protection unit or whatever, and he was saying that was in charge of making sure the streets were swept properly, but that didn't go on for very long, and I left immediately after. And then there was another time he got drunk and he nearly killed me. I was with another guy who was a Serb, and he told that guy not to hang out with me because I might be killed, and then he made some other threats, but then another man whom I didn't know came along, and he saved me from Mitar and took me back home. This was something that was happening before we left for Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you just indicated to me that you learned who Mitar was in terms of him being at the Behija Zukic funeral after you left to Macedonia. How did you find that out after you left to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I believe that misstates the witness's previous testimony on line 23 at page 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us how it misstates it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The question posed said after he left for Macedonia. The witness just indicated that he learned it before he left for Macedonia. Page 25, line 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me -- Witness, who did you learn who Mitar was? Was it before you left for Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I left, when he got hold of us outside in the street and made us clean the streets. I was just walking down the street, but it was before I left for Macedonia and not after that I learned. It was between the 21st of May and the beginning of June, which was the time we set off for Macedonia. It was at that time that I realised who Mitar was, and I heard that he was a waiter at Panos. I heard this from the local Muslims who knew him better than me, and the same local Muslims who he also made clean the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But I guess more specifically what I'm asking you is, who told you that Mitar was at the Behija Zukic funeral, and when did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: When we left the funeral, my friend and I, it was then that we discussed this, who that man was and who knew him. I didn't know him well enough, but my friend knew him much better than I did because that man had made his brother clean the streets before, and he even went to their home to call him to come out and clean the streets. And then my friend told me, "This is the person who came for Samir to make him clean the streets when he actually came to their flat," and that's when I realised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you were discussing this as the people were being herded into the truck or later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And are you telling me that Samir could recognise Mitar Vasiljevic from a hundred and fifty metres away, more than -- much more than a football field's length?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Not Samir, Almir. Almir recognised him, and he later said that he was the man who had come for Samir, and that's why he recognised him. He probably came to their home in that same suit or whatever. I don't know exactly what happened. I just know that he told me that he had come for his brother and that he had forced him to clean the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But that's a separate issue. I understand why your brother might know someone as he knocks on his door and tells him to come out and clean the streets, but what I'm -- what I want to understand is how Almir can recognise a man a hundred and fifty metres away.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I've said it about four times, I believe. Maybe it was less than 150 metres. I said so in my statement. It was in the roughest of terms. It may have been less. It's very difficult for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would you agree that it's difficult to recognise a person from one end of a football field to another without binoculars?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe you have different concepts of what is a football field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's true. I do, Your Honour. But I think of a hundred metres as sort of the average length, but I agree; it is a little longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's have the witness's answer, and let us move on, move away from this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My friend said this was the same person who had knocked at his door, and that's how we realised that the person was Mitar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Since you were not -- since you were approached to give the interview in 1995, is it true that the interviewers gave you names of suspects in Visegrad of which they wanted to question you about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So they didn't suggest to you that they wanted to ask you about a Milan Lukic or a Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: They just asked about what had happened at the bridge. They -- they weren't asking any questions about the rest or how Milan Lukic killed those kids. That's what they asked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so as you were first approached, they asked you about Milan Lukic specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you didn't bring up that name on your own, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I certainly did. I was the first to drop his name, and it wasn't before such time that they asked me about that person. The people who were asking me these questions didn't even know about him. It was after I'd brought him up myself that they asked if he was from Visegrad and if I knew where he was from, that sort of thing. They didn't know who had killed those persons until I told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But isn't it true that the name of Milan Lukic had been talked about before this interview amongst you, your family, and members of your community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I think the whole town of Visegrad was mentioning him. He killed half the town, probably. In my presence, he killed two kids. That's all I can say because that's what I saw. I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you were getting ready to get on the bus convoy and you're with your sister's friend who spoke with this man named Milan, you had never seen this man before that day, never been introduced to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection, compound question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't see it as compounded. Had you seen -- had you been introduced to that person before, before that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that day, I didn't know the name of that person. I had just seen him, one, at a distance, and I wasn't sure who he was until I saw him next, and on that occasion the picture came back to me, and I recognised him from the occasion at the cemetery when I had seen him earlier. I hadn't learned his name until my friend's sister addressed him and he took me away, brought me to the prison and said, "None of these people here are allowed to touch you. It's Milan Lukic's order."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you ever see a brown Passat in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you notice any other Passats in Visegrad of any colour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Passat, the kind that the Zukic family had, I had never seen driven or owned by anyone else. Maybe there was similar Passat 20 years old, but nobody else had a new Passat of any colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you -- of your sister's friend that talked to this Milan, did -- how old was she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: The same age as Milan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How old is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: I think around 25, 26. I don't know. I didn't ask her.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you have information of when she graduated from secondary school or the year of her birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: No. I wasn't that close friends with her. I was friends with her brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when she called him and spoke to him, she only used the first name. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: At first when she addressed him, she said Milan, but later after he asked her something, she said Milan Lukic. At any rate, they were talking about school, their class, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And other than this person, you would not have had a name to a face? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Right. Otherwise, I wouldn't know the name of that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And regardless -- and at any other time during your encounters with the police or your stay at the police station or your ride on the bridge, no one ever addressed each other by names. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Correct. Those Serbs in the car did not use names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. I'm almost done. I have nothing further, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alarid. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: VG-89, you were asked some questions about where you were kept at the police station between the 14th of June and the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the court usher could please call up photograph under 65 ter number 178.29.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: VG-89, directing your attention to the photograph that now appears before you, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is it a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: It's inside the MUP building in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Does this photograph truly and accurately depict the inside area of the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Correct. This is from -- taken from the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please describe the stairs and where they lead in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: These stairs start from the very entrance into the building. They lead upstairs, and this glazed room with the frame painted blue is the reception area where I was first led when Milan Lukic brought me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution would tender this exhibit into evidence, 65 ter number 178.29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as Exhibit P104, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the court officer could please call up 65 ter number 178.31.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: VG-89, directing your attention to the photograph that now appears before you, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: The inside of that reception area, and the other white door over there leads into the office where they put the knife under my throat on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Does this photograph truly and accurately depict the reception area and the other office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was this the initial area in which Milan Lukic brought you when you arrived on the 14th of June, 1992, this reception area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution offers 65 ter number 178.31 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as P105, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the court usher could please call up 65 ter number 178.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: VG-89, directing your attention to the photograph that now appears before you. Do you recognise what's depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What does this photograph depict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: This first room on the right with the door open is the one where I spent those three days. Facing it is the lavatory where this man Lelek took me and filled the bottle of water for me. The room on the right is where I spent the three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Does this photograph true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why didn't you do this in examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the last photograph. I was conscientious of time, and it was brought up in -- I believe, based on cross-examination there was some lack of charity as to the set-up of the police station, so the Prosecution at this time is clarifying the cross-examination that was conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, with a very liberal interpretation of how it arises, yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: VG-89, you mentioned that you were in this area on this floor throughout the entire time that you were there. Were you able to see the entrance from the spot in which you were being kept while at the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-89
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to see the street through the small window; and through this open door, which was barred, I could see the police and the paramilitaries passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, before you call the next witness, may I ask whether you have any evidence forthcoming that will tell us about the fate of the red Passat?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness, Your Honour, is VG- --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Alarid, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just housekeeping, Your Honour. I did want to tender 2D01-0143 and 2D01-0152, which is the '95 statement under seal; and I would tender 1D10-1679 and 1D10-1690, which is the January 2001 statement, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure whether the court deputy got all of that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The numbers are not in the transcript entirely, Your Honours, but the 1995 statement will become 1D47, and January 2001 statement will become 1D48. Both under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I'll ask both parties -- or all parties to make an effort to remember to have the documents tendered during their examination. Yes, Mr. Weber. Are you also a culprit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted one other housekeeping matter too. I don't know if it was clear whether or not the Prosecution formally tendered 65 ter number 178.30, the last photograph, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be admitted as P106, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is VG-63. If it doesn't distract the court too much, I'd just like to switch some personnel here in the courtroom. There are a few matters -- the attorney who will be handing this witness is just outside the door. If I might use this time, Your Honour, before the witness is called in, there are a couple of matters I'd like to raise with the Chamber while the witness is being brought in and...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The first is, Your Honour, with respect to VG-002, I've carefully reviewed it this morning, and just assessing the overall evidence that the Chamber has heard, I'm no longer certain that it's essential evidence that need be before the Chamber. I think what we intended to elicit through this witness has been established both with the Chamber's decision in adjudicated facts on other witnesses. So the Prosecution will be withdrawing that witness or not be calling the evidence of that witness, and I will be filing a written application with respect to that. Your Honour, I'm also conscious of the fact that this present witness as well as this upcoming witness I anticipate may take in excess of the time that we originally estimated. I believe that -- I mean, again, these are simply estimates, but there is -- it occurs to me that there's one other way that we could shorten the case and remain on track, and that's the third witness that's planned to be called is VG-16, and the attorney who's been working with him finds him very traumatised. He's an elderly man. He's actually the father of one of the boys who you've heard was killed at the bridge, and we -- and I'm asking, would the Court entertain an oral motion to convert his mode of testimony to 92 ter. We would lead any of his evidence that deals with the accused, but in terms of the other information not directly dealing with the accused, would the Court entertain an application by the Prosecution to amend the mode of testimony? I think in this way we could take his testimony much more briefly. One of the concerns of the attorney taking him is that he's very, very long-winded and hard to control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, before I rule, let me just hear Mr. Alarid and Mr. Cepic on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We would object to the 92 ter placement, Your Honours. It was not tendered in advance, so we would ask that they hold to the viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When is that witness due?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He's the witness after this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: After this. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I would just note, I've looked at 92 ter. Although the practice is that it is done in a pleading procedure before trial, there is nothing in the rule that requires it to be done that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I feel we can meet their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, are you disadvantaged in any way? Are you prejudiced in any way? I don't see how you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, only -- and only in so much as sometimes the original recollection of a witness is something that the Court needs to observe, and in this particular case considering the fact that the counts against my client were not necessarily the same as Mr. Vasiljevic or -- or before, that to a certain degree he would be touching on brand new evidence of which I don't think that the Prosecution should be obliged to lead through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, related to VG-16, no objection for the mode of testimony pursuant to Rule 92 ter. And with your leave, just if I may say just one sentence related to VG-63, just for the record I think -- this is my humble opinion that this witness is not relevant for this indictment. Just for the record. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just to bring the Court's attention, Your Honour, with VG-16 there are two statements, the January 6th, 1995, statement and the April 10, 1997, statement that the English translations are pending, and so that also kind of adds to the difficulty of doing it 93 ter when we have two statements with the English translation pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Groome, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm addressing that issue with Mr. Van Hooydonk at the moment, but I'm not sure that really would change anything. If the English translations are not available in a timely fashion, of course we'll hold the witness for as long as necessary so Mr. Alarid has a full opportunity to cross-examine him on those. Your Honour, I would point out, just -- I think there was a bit of a misstatement. He did not testify in the Vasiljevic case. The only prior -- or the written evidence that we would be submitting would be his ICTY statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber accepts the submission made by the Prosecution to convert VG-16 to a 92 ter statement, and it also accepts the withdrawal of witness -- what was the name of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: VG-002, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: VG-002, yes. Closed session for the forthcoming witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
